promptText: What is the key difference between a "component library" and a "design system"?
options: A component library is just the code artifact (the components); a design system additionally includes design tokens, usage guidelines, accessibility standards, and the governance process that keeps design and engineering in sync
They are interchangeable terms describing the same deliverable, just used by different teams
A design system only exists inside Figma, while a component library only exists in code, with no connection between the two
A component library is always built with Tailwind, while a design system is always built with CSS-in-JS
explanation: A component library is the most visible artifact of a design system, but a design system also encompasses design tokens as a single source of truth, patterns, guidelines, and governance -- without which components and Figma files drift out of sync over time.

promptText: In a tiered design token system (global -> semantic/alias -> component), why should components reference only semantic tokens like `--color-bg-primary` rather than raw global tokens like `--blue-500` directly?
options: So a rebrand or theme change only requires re-pointing the semantic alias to a new raw value in one place, instead of finding and replacing every raw value reference across every component that happened to use it
Because CSS does not allow a component's stylesheet to reference a raw color value directly under any circumstances
Semantic tokens are required by the CSS specification for any property that affects color or spacing
Global tokens are deprecated in modern CSS and will be removed from browsers in a future version
explanation: The semantic tier decouples what a value is from what it means. If ten components reference --blue-500 directly for ten different purposes, a rebrand can't just change --blue-500 without side effects; but if they all reference --color-bg-primary, remapping that one alias updates every consumer automatically.

promptText: A `Tabs` component is implemented as a compound component (`<Tabs><Tabs.List><Tabs.Tab/></Tabs.List><Tabs.Panel/></Tabs>`) using React Context internally. What problem does this solve compared to a single `Tabs` component with props like `tabs`, `activeIndex`, `onTabChange`, `showIcons`, `iconPosition`?
options: It avoids prop explosion by letting consumers control layout and content directly with JSX, while the shared state (which tab is active) is passed implicitly via context instead of being threaded through an ever-growing configuration prop
It makes the component render faster because Context updates never cause re-renders
It eliminates the need for the component to manage any internal state at all
It is required because React does not allow object props to contain more than three keys
explanation: As a single component grows more layout/content variants, it tends toward an unmaintainable pile of interacting boolean and config props. Compound components let consumers freely arrange, omit, or wrap subcomponents in JSX while the parent shares state implicitly through context -- new layouts are expressed by rearranging markup, not by adding new props.

promptText: A team is building their own in-house design system from scratch and needs an accessible dialog, combobox, and menu. Why would they typically build these on top of a headless library like Radix Primitives rather than fully-styled components from MUI or Chakra?
options: Headless libraries provide correct accessibility and interaction behavior with zero visual opinion, so the team can invest their engineering effort in their own tokens and visual layer instead of fighting to re-skin someone else's default theme
Fully-styled libraries like MUI cannot be customized at all, so they are unusable for any real product
Headless libraries are always smaller in bundle size than any fully-styled library, which is the primary reason to choose them
Radix Primitives ship with a complete visual theme that matches most companies' brand guidelines out of the box
explanation: Headless libraries solve the hard, easy-to-get-wrong problem of accessible interaction logic (focus trapping, roving tabindex, ARIA wiring) with no CSS opinion, which is exactly what a team building its own design system wants -- they don't have to fight a fully-styled library's default theme to make it look like their own product.

promptText: A well-designed `Switch` component in a component library should support both `<Switch defaultValue={false} onChange={fn} />` (uncontrolled) and `<Switch value={checked} onChange={setChecked} />` (controlled). What determines which mode the component operates in?
options: Whether the `value` prop is passed at all -- if defined, the component treats itself as controlled and always renders that prop; if undefined, it manages its own internal state seeded from defaultValue
The component must be explicitly told which mode to use via a separate `controlled` boolean prop
React automatically detects which mode to use based on whether the component is wrapped in a form element
Uncontrolled mode is only available in class components, so a function component like this must always be controlled
explanation: A common shared hook pattern (often called useControllableState) checks whether `value !== undefined`; if so it always renders the passed-in value (controlled), and otherwise falls back to internal state seeded by defaultValue (uncontrolled) -- mirroring how native <input> already works with value vs defaultValue.

promptText: Why is it accurate to describe Storybook stories as documentation that "cannot go stale"?
options: A story is code that renders the actual component with real props, so the documentation is literally the component running, not separate prose that can drift out of sync with the real implementation
Storybook automatically rewrites its own markdown documentation every time a component's source code changes
Stories are compiled directly into a component's TypeScript type definitions, making them impossible to write incorrectly
Storybook prevents developers from merging any pull request that doesn't also update the documentation
explanation: Unlike a wiki page or README that describes behavior in prose and can silently drift from reality, a story is executable code rendering the real component -- if the component's actual behavior changes, the story either still accurately demonstrates it or visibly breaks, rather than quietly becoming inaccurate.

promptText: Why does fixing an accessibility bug (e.g., a missing focus trap) inside a shared design-system Modal component have disproportionately high leverage compared to fixing the same bug in one app's custom modal?
options: Because every consuming team inherits the fix automatically the next time they update the dependency, so the cost is paid once in the shared component while the benefit compounds across every product surface that uses it
Because design-system components are exempt from needing further accessibility testing once a fix ships
Because shared components are rendered on the server, which automatically resolves all focus-management issues
Because accessibility bugs only matter in components that are used by more than five different teams
explanation: A design system is a leverage point: the same bug fixed once in a shared Button or Modal propagates to every consuming app on the next version bump, whereas leaving accessibility to each app team means the same class of bug gets independently (and inconsistently) discovered and fixed, or not fixed, N separate times.

promptText: A pull request causes Chromatic to flag visual diffs across 40 stories after a shared token change. A junior engineer treats this as a failing test that must be reverted. What is the more accurate way to interpret a visual regression diff?
options: It is a prompt for human review, not necessarily a bug -- the diff could be the intended, expected effect of the token change and just needs to be approved as the new baseline, distinguishing it from a functional test's simple pass/fail
Visual regression tools can only detect layout bugs, never legitimate intentional visual changes, so any diff always indicates a real defect
Chromatic automatically determines whether a diff is intentional or a bug using AI, so no human review step is ever required
The diff means the PR's unit tests are broken and must be rewritten before the visual snapshots can be regenerated
explanation: Visual regression testing catches unintended pixel-level changes, but unlike a functional test it requires human judgment to distinguish 'this is an intentional design update, approve the new baseline' from 'this is an unintended side effect, fix the underlying change' -- a shared token change rippling into 40 components could easily be the correct, intended outcome.

promptText: A design system package lists `styled-components` as a regular dependency (not a peer dependency) and is consumed by many apps with heterogeneous stacks. What specific risk does this create that CSS Modules or a zero-runtime CSS-in-JS tool would avoid?
options: A consuming app that also uses styled-components at a different version can end up with two separate styled-components runtimes bundled at once, causing mismatched theme contexts or styles that silently fail to apply
styled-components cannot be published inside any npm package under any circumstances
CSS Modules have no way to scope class names, so they would create the exact same risk regardless of dependency type
Zero-runtime CSS-in-JS tools require every consuming app to install the same version of React, which styled-components does not
explanation: Declaring a CSS-in-JS runtime library as a plain dependency (rather than a peer dependency with a documented supported range) risks two independent runtime instances coexisting in one bundle if the consumer uses a different version -- causing duplicated CSS-in-JS engines, mismatched ThemeProvider contexts, or styles that silently don't apply. CSS Modules and zero-runtime tools produce plain CSS with no such runtime coupling.

promptText: A design system uses Changesets for releases. What is the actual mechanism by which a contributor's PR ends up producing a published npm version with an accurate changelog?
options: The contributor adds a small changeset file describing the change and its semver bump in their PR; a bot aggregates pending changesets into a standing 'Version Packages' PR that bumps versions and writes the changelog, and merging that PR triggers the actual publish
Changesets automatically infers the correct semver bump by analyzing the git diff with no human input required at any point
Every merged PR to main is published as its own separate npm version immediately, with the version number chosen at random
Changesets replaces semantic versioning entirely with a simple incrementing build number that has no relationship to breaking changes
explanation: The Changesets workflow has each contributing PR include a changeset describing its own semver bump; a bot then opens/updates an aggregating 'Version Packages' PR with the accumulated bumps and generated changelog entries, and merging that PR is what actually triggers `changeset publish` in CI -- removing 'what version should this be' from human memory.

promptText: A design system needs to rename a widely-used `Button` prop from `size` to `variant`. What is the correct rollout sequence?
options: Keep the old `size` prop working while emitting a development-only warning pointing at `variant`, provide a codemod for mechanical migration, and only actually remove `size` in a subsequent major version after a real migration window
Immediately remove `size` and replace it with `variant` in the next patch release, since prop renames are not considered breaking changes
Publish two entirely separate npm packages, one with the old API and one with the new API, and require every consumer to choose permanently
Silently support both prop names forever with no warning or documentation, so no team is ever forced to migrate
explanation: A breaking API change should never ship silently in a patch or minor release. The deprecation lifecycle is: announce and support both APIs, add a dev-only warning pointing at the migration path, offer an automated codemod for the mechanical rename, and remove the old API only in a major version bump that consumers opt into deliberately.

promptText: A design system built entirely by a platform team in isolation, with no involvement from feature teams during development, launches to low adoption -- teams keep using their own existing components instead. What does this scenario primarily illustrate?
options: Adoption failure is usually a people and process problem, not a code-quality problem -- by the time a system built without early adopter involvement launches, teams have already built working alternatives and see no reason to migrate
The design system's components must have had bugs, since adoption failures are always caused by poor code quality
The platform team should have used a fully-styled library like MUI instead of building custom components
Cross-team adoption is impossible unless the design system is mandated by executive order from day one
explanation: The most common failure mode for design systems is being built in isolation without early adopter buy-in: by the time it ships, feature teams have already solved their own problems and have no incentive to migrate to something that arrived too late and wasn't shaped by their actual needs -- a governance and process failure, not necessarily a quality one.

promptText: A Style Dictionary pipeline includes a custom transform that converts a spacing token's raw pixel value to rem for the web platform output (e.g. 16px -> 1rem). Beyond code cleanliness, what user-facing property does this specific transform choice actually protect?
options: Accessibility -- rem-based sizing scales proportionally with a user's browser-level base font-size preference, whereas hardcoded px values stay visually frozen regardless of that accessibility setting
SEO ranking, since search engines penalize any stylesheet that uses pixel units for spacing
Build performance, since rem values compile faster than pixel values in every CSS bundler
Cross-browser compatibility, since older browsers cannot parse pixel units at all
explanation: This is a case where a low-level build-pipeline decision has a direct accessibility consequence: if a user increases their browser's default font size for readability, rem-based values (relative to the root font-size) scale accordingly, while px-based values remain fixed -- so the token transform is quietly enforcing an accessibility guarantee across every component that consumes spacing/sizing tokens.

promptText: A design system's `Button` component supports `asChild` (Radix's Slot pattern) so `` renders an actual `` tag with Button's styling and click behavior. Why is this preferred over the design system adding an `as="a" | "NextLink" | "RouterLink"` string prop enumerating known routing components?
options: The design system cannot know in advance every consuming app's routing library (Next.js Link, React Router Link, a custom internal Link, plain anchor), so asChild shifts control of the actual rendered element to the consumer while the component still contributes styling and merges its behavior onto whatever element is provided
String-based `as` props are not supported by TypeScript, so asChild is the only type-safe option available
asChild is faster at runtime because it avoids calling React.cloneElement, unlike an `as` prop implementation
asChild removes the need for the component to forward refs, since Slot never needs access to the underlying DOM node
explanation: An enumerable `as` prop requires the design system to anticipate and maintain support for every possible consumer routing/link primitive, which doesn't scale across an organization with many apps and frameworks. asChild inverts the responsibility: the consumer supplies and fully controls the actual element, and Slot merges the component's className, event handlers (composed, not overwritten), and ref onto that child -- which is also why the prop-merging logic in Slot has to carefully combine rather than overwrite conflicting props.

promptText: A component's API has grown to include `isPrimary`, `isDanger`, `isSmall`, `isLarge`, `hasIcon`, and `iconOnLeft` as six independent boolean props. A senior engineer proposes refactoring to `variant: "primary" | "secondary" | "danger"`, `size: "sm" | "md" | "lg"`, and letting the icon be passed as a child. What is the core problem being fixed, framed precisely?
options: The boolean props allow semantically invalid combinations to be constructed (like isPrimary && isDanger both true) that every consumer and test then has to account for; closed enums and composition make those invalid states structurally unrepresentable instead of merely discouraged by convention
Boolean props are slower to evaluate at runtime than string enum comparisons, so the refactor is purely a performance optimization
React limits function components to a maximum of four boolean props before requiring a class component
The refactor is only about reducing the number of characters typed in JSX, with no effect on the space of possible component states
explanation: Independent booleans can combine freely, including into combinations that were never designed or tested (isPrimary and isDanger simultaneously true). A closed enum like variant makes such combinations a type error rather than a runtime possibility -- 'making invalid states unrepresentable' -- while pushing icon placement into composition (a child) removes props whose validity depended on another prop's value (iconOnLeft only matters if hasIcon is true).
